claims.text: Well-dispersed graphene nanoplatelets placed at tungsten–copper interfaces will increase the overall thermal conductivity of a W–Cu composite.
The graphene nanoplatelets will reduce interfacial thermal resistance between tungsten and copper.
The graphene intervention will not compromise the composite's mechanical durability.
The graphene intervention will not compromise the composite's irradiation resistance.
Graphene nanoplatelets at W–Cu boundaries will enhance coupling between the tungsten and copper phases.
Graphene nanoplatelets possess ultrahigh intrinsic thermal conductivity.
Interfacial graphene nanoplatelets create additional heat-transfer pathways between tungsten and copper.
Poor bonding between tungsten and copper is a bottleneck for heat transfer in the baseline composite.
The two-dimensional morphology of graphene nanoplatelets can preserve mechanical interlocking in the composite.
The two-dimensional morphology of graphene nanoplatelets can preserve resistance to irradiation-induced defects.
The graphene-enhanced composite will show a moderate percentage increase in thermal conductivity relative to an otherwise identically processed W–Cu composite without graphene.
The graphene-enhanced composite will retain mechanical strength comparable to the baseline composite.
The graphene-enhanced composite will retain irradiation resistance comparable to the baseline composite.
The beneficial effect requires graphene nanoplatelets to be optimally dispersed at a controlled loading.
Excessive graphene loading or poor graphene dispersion may degrade mechanical properties.
Excessive graphene loading or poor graphene dispersion may reduce irradiation tolerance.
